findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit request context and are canceled when the request ends
findings.body: Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection start legacy writes in goroutines using the handler's request context. Go's HTTP server cancels that context as soon as ServeHTTP returns, so these goroutines will frequently begin with an already-canceled context and the legacy write will fail immediately. The 10-second timeout added inside the goroutine does not help because its parent is already canceled. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (to preserve values such as user/tenant) or a writer-scoped background context before spawning the goroutine.

findings.title: Async legacy writes are unordered and can overwrite newer state
findings.body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no sequencing. Two successive updates to the same object can reach legacy storage out of order, and an update can run before the create that preceded it. Legacy storage can therefore end up with older data than unified storage even when both operations succeed, which defeats the purpose of the safety copy. This needs ordered delivery (for example a per-object or per-resource queue) or a different fallback strategy.

findings.title: Legacy update recomputes the update from the legacy object instead of using the stored result
findings.body: Storage.Update computes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the unified-storage old object. The async legacy path then passes the original objInfo again, so Legacy.Update calls UpdatedObject against the legacy store's old object. For patches/applies or any UpdatedObjectInfo that depends on the current object, the two stores can produce different results and diverge. The previous implementation explicitly wrapped objInfo with the object returned from unified storage; this path should pass a wrapper carrying the storage result (res) instead of the raw objInfo.

findings.title: Mode 3 records several metrics with the wrong recorder or arguments
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified-storage failures are reported as legacy failures and no storage failure metric is emitted. Update has the same bug at line 129. Delete at line 106 passes the object name as the kind label, producing incorrect and potentially high-cardinality kind values. DeleteCollection at line 166 records the legacy goroutine's result with recordStorageDuration, double-counting storage metrics. These make the dual-writer metrics unreliable for diagnosing mode-3 behavior.

findings.title: Async legacy write failures are silently dropped
findings.body: The async Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines only feed legacy errors into a metric; no log is emitted. If legacy writes fail because of context cancellation, validation, conflicts, or storage errors, operators get no explicit indication that unified and legacy storage have diverged. At least log the error with kind/name and the fact that it occurred on the async legacy path.

findings.title: Mode 3 Create error test mocks legacy instead of unified storage
findings.body: The error case for TestMode3_Create configures setupLegacyFn to return an error, but mode 3 calls Storage.Create first. There is no expectation set for the storage mock, so the test will panic on an unexpected mock call instead of exercising the intended storage-error path. This case needs setupStorageFn returning the error (and should leave legacy unconfigured because it should not be called).

findings.title: Delete and DeleteCollection tests spawn async legacy calls that are neither mocked nor awaited
findings.body: TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection only configure storage expectations. On success, mode 3 launches a goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Delete or d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but the legacy mock has no matching expectation and the test does not wait for the goroutine. That leads to a panic from testify's mock (often asynchronously) and the assertions do not verify that the legacy write happened at all. The tests need legacy mock expectations plus a synchronization mechanism (or an injectable executor) for the async operation.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy propagation
findings.body: The new mode-3 cases run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which creates/updates via the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists or gets the same data through the legacy API and requires exact equality. Mode 3 intentionally writes to legacy asynchronously, so legacy may not have caught up yet and the test will be flaky or fail. These checks need eventual-consistency polling or should not assert immediate legacy visibility for mode 3.
